extracted.intended_audience: general readers, film fans, researchers looking for encyclopedic information about the film
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article summarizing The Hangover Part III: plot, cast, production, release, box office, critical response, and awards. It provides factual and evaluative material about the 2013 comedy film.

rubrics_metrics.name: Box office / commercial performance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hangover Part III grossed $112.2 million in North America and $249.8 million in other territories for a total of $362 million, against a budget of $103 million; making it the lowest-grossing film of the trilogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page reports projections and actuals: projected to earn $80 million in its first four days but grossed $53.5 million over its first four days (including $41.7M opening), and earned $3.1 million in late Wednesday night screenings. Comparisons to prior installments (Part II's $135 million opening days) and contemporaneous releases (Fast & Furious 6) are used to contextualize commercial success or underperformance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate critic scores (Rotten Tomatoes / Metacritic / CinemaScore)
rubrics_metrics.description: On Rotten Tomatoes, the film has an approval percentage of 21% based on 202 reviews, with the critics consensus: "Less a comedy than an angrily dark action thriller, The Hangover Part III diverges from the series' rote formula but offers nothing compelling in its place." On Metacritic the film has a score of 30 out of 100 based on 37 critic reviews, meaning "Generally Unfavorable." Audiences polled by CinemaScore gave the film an average grade of "B" on an A+ to F scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These numerical/aggregated metrics are presented as measures of critical and audience reception; the Rotten Tomatoes consensus sentence is reported verbatim to summarize critical judgment. Use of multiple aggregators provides both critic and audience perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical qualitative assessments (tone, genre consistency, narrative/structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics described the film as diverging from the series' formula and questioned whether it should be considered a comedy at all. Examples: Variety called it 'Less a comedy than an angrily dark action thriller'; Andrew Barker said it 'more often plays like a loopily plotted, exposition-heavy actioner.' Stephen Farber wrote that young viewers seeking 'unbridled raunch' will be disappointed; The New York Times called it 'a dull, lazy walkthrough.' Christy Lemire noted it 'runs a different sort of risk by going to darker and more dangerous places.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualitative critical remarks are used to evaluate whether the film succeeds tonally and artistically—particularly whether the tone departs from expectations of the franchise and how that affects comedic value. Multiple critic quotes illustrate common themes: darker tone, departure from previous installments' structure, and perceived lack of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards, nominations, and industry recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominations: 40th People's Choice Awards (Favorite Comedic Movie; Favorite Comedic Movie Actor nominations), teaser trailer nominated for Best Comedy at the 2013 Golden Trailer Awards, nominated for Worst Remake, Rip-off or Sequel at the 34th Golden Raspberry Awards, Sequel or Remake That Shouldn't Have Been Made at 2013 Alliance of Women Film Journalists Awards, Hollywood Film Award nomination at the 17th Hollywood Film Awards. Location manager Gregory Alpert won Location Professional of the Year – Features at the 2013 California On Location Awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listing of awards/nominations serves to document industry and popular recognition, both positive and negative (including Razzie-style negative awards). Individual wins (e.g., location manager award) and nominations provide another axis of evaluation beyond box office and critic scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting, star participation, and production staffing
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal actors Bradley Cooper, Zach Galifianakis, and Ed Helms re-signed to reprise roles with reports they were nearing deals receiving $15 million (against the backend) each. The page documents cast returns (Ken Jeong, Heather Graham, Sasha Barrese, Justin Bartha), and additions/negotiations (John Goodman, Melissa McCarthy, Mike Epps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Casting and salary/contract details indicate investment in star power and can be used to assess production priorities and expectations. Expanded roles (e.g., Ken Jeong's significantly expanded role) and late negotiations are relevant to evaluating how casting choices may influence the film's tone and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production, filming locations, and release strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal photography began September 10, 2012 in Los Angeles, moved to Nogales, Arizona (doubling as Tijuana), then Las Vegas, concluding November 16, 2012. Warner Bros. moved the U.S. release to May 23, 2013 to attempt to beat the Memorial Day weekend rush and compete with Universal's Fast & Furious 6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production timeline, choice of filming locations, and release-date strategy are documented as contextual factors that may affect film logistics, marketing, and box-office performance. The page reports specific closures and location shoots (e.g., California State Route 73 closure) that reflect production scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundtrack and featured music as stylistic/content element
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hangover Part III: Original Motion Picture Soundtrack released May 21, 2013; track listing includes songs by Hanson, Billy Joel, Nine Inch Nails (featured but not on soundtrack), Black Sabbath, Kanye West, Phil Collins, and others. Total soundtrack length listed as 39:49.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music selection and soundtrack release are presented as components of the film's aesthetic and marketing; notable inclusions and omissions (songs featured in the film but not on the soundtrack) are recorded and can be used to evaluate the film's tonal choices and audience appeal.
